whatIsSystemDesign.title: What is a System Design Interview?
whatIsSystemDesign.description: A system design interview tests your ability to architect large-scale distributed systems. Unlike coding interviews that focus on algorithms, system design evaluates how you think about building real-world applications that can handle millions of users.

keyPoints.title: Not About Perfect Answers
keyPoints.description: There's no single 'right' answer. Interviewers want to see your thought process, how you make trade-offs, and how you communicate complex ideas.

keyPoints.title: Evaluates Senior-Level Thinking
keyPoints.description: This interview separates senior engineers from juniors. It tests your experience with scalability, reliability, and real-world constraints.

keyPoints.title: Communication is Half the Battle
keyPoints.description: How you explain your design matters as much as the design itself. Clear communication shows leadership potential.

methodology.title: The IFRAILST Framework
methodology.subtitle: A structured 8-step approach to tackle any system design question
methodology.description: After coaching 200+ engineers, I've developed this repeatable framework that ensures you cover all the bases while keeping your interview on track. Each letter represents a critical pillar of system design.

steps.name: Intent & Users
steps.description: Clarify scope & assumptions. Define who uses the system, their goals, scale expectations, and constraints.

steps.name: Functional & Non-Functional
steps.description: Define what the system must do (features, workflows) and how well it must do it (SLA, latency, durability).

steps.name: Rates, Scale & Growth
steps.description: Quantify read/write QPS, data growth, cache hit ratios, and traffic patterns. All architecture decisions depend on scale.

steps.name: Architecture & Boundaries
steps.description: Draw the core architecture with 5-8 labeled components. Explain data flow and failure boundaries.

steps.name: Interfaces & Data Model
steps.description: Define APIs (REST/GraphQL/gRPC), data schemas, indexing, partitioning, and versioning strategy.

steps.name: Latency, Reliability & Resilience
steps.description: Quantify p95/p99 latency targets. Define failover, retries, circuit breakers, and disaster recovery (RPO/RTO).

steps.name: Security
steps.description: Authentication (OAuth2/IAM), authorization (RBAC/ABAC), encryption (TLS/KMS), rate limiting, and audit logging.

steps.name: Trade-offs, Testing & Telemetry
steps.description: Highlight 2-3 explicit trade-offs. Define metrics to track, chaos/load testing strategy, and alerting setup.

faqs.question: How should I organize my system design answer?
faqs.answer: Start by clarifying requirements (2-3 minutes), then move to high-level architecture, API design, and database schema. Save 5-10 minutes at the end for discussing trade-offs and scaling considerations. Never start drawing before understanding what you're building.

faqs.question: How much time should I spend on each part?
faqs.answer: For a 45-minute interview: Requirements gathering (5 min), high-level design (15 min), deep dive into 1-2 components (15 min), trade-offs and scaling (10 min). Adjust based on interviewer signals—if they want to go deeper on something, follow their lead.

faqs.question: Should I start with requirements or the architecture diagram?
faqs.answer: Always start with requirements. Jumping to diagrams is the #1 mistake I see. Asking clarifying questions shows maturity and prevents you from designing the wrong thing. Spend 3-5 minutes understanding functional and non-functional requirements before picking up the marker.

faqs.question: Should I keep talking continuously or pause for discussion?
faqs.answer: Strike a balance. Don't monologue for 20 minutes, but don't pause every 30 seconds asking 'is this okay?' Check in at natural transition points: after requirements, after high-level design, before going deep. This creates dialogue and lets you adjust based on feedback.

faqs.question: How deep should I go into the architecture?
faqs.answer: Start broad (boxes and arrows), then go deep on 1-2 critical components the interviewer cares about. Going deep on everything is impossible in 45 minutes. Let the interviewer guide which areas to explore. Depth in the right areas shows expertise; depth everywhere shows poor prioritization.

faqs.question: What if I don't know a specific technology they ask about?
faqs.answer: Be honest, then pivot to what you know. Say 'I haven't worked with X directly, but I'm familiar with Y which solves similar problems.' Interviewers value honesty and the ability to reason about solutions over memorized technology names.

faqs.question: How do I handle scale questions if I've never built systems at FAANG scale?
faqs.answer: Focus on principles, not experience. Understand horizontal scaling, database sharding, caching strategies, and load balancing conceptually. Practice back-of-envelope calculations. I've helped many engineers from smaller companies ace these questions through targeted practice.

faqs.question: What are the most common system design questions for senior roles?
faqs.answer: Design a URL shortener, design Twitter/Instagram feed, design a chat system, design a rate limiter, design a distributed cache, design a notification system. For principal/staff roles, expect more ambiguous problems like 'design our cloud infrastructure' where scoping is crucial.

architectureDiagrams.title: System Design Architecture Patterns
architectureDiagrams.description: Master these fundamental patterns that appear in nearly every FAANG system design interview. Understanding these building blocks helps you tackle any design question.

diagrams.title: Read-Heavy Service Pattern
diagrams.subtitle: URL Shortener, Config Service, Feature Flags
diagrams.description: Optimized for services with high read-to-write ratio (100:1 or more). Uses multi-layer caching and read replicas to handle massive read traffic.

diagrams.title: Real-Time Messaging Pattern
diagrams.subtitle: Chat Apps, Notifications, Collaboration Tools
diagrams.description: Handles bidirectional real-time communication with persistent connections. Requires connection management and message delivery guarantees.

diagrams.title: Feed & Ranking Pattern
diagrams.subtitle: Social Media Feed, News Aggregation, Recommendations
diagrams.description: Generates personalized content feeds using ML ranking. Balances precomputation (push) vs on-demand (pull) based on user follower counts.

diagrams.title: Distributed Storage Pattern
diagrams.subtitle: Object Storage, File Systems, Data Lakes
diagrams.description: Stores massive amounts of data across multiple nodes with replication and partitioning. Handles node failures gracefully.
